articles.title: Advancing Embodied Intelligence in Robotic-Assisted Endovascular Procedures: A Systematic Review of AI Solutions
articles.content: Endovascular procedures have revolutionized vascular disease treatment, yet their manual execution is challenged by the demands for high precision, operator fatigue, and radiation exposure. Robotic systems have emerged as transformative solutions to mitigate these inherent limitations. A crucial moment has arrived, where a confluence of pressing clinical needs and breakthroughs in AI creates an opportunity for a paradigm shift toward Embodied Intelligence (EI), enabling robots to navigate complex vascular networks and adapt to dynamic physiological conditions. Data-driven approaches, leveraging advanced computer vision, medical image analysis, and machine learning, drive this evolution by enabling real-time vessel segmentation, device tracking, and anatomical landmark detection. Reinforcement learning and imitation learning further improve navigation strategies and replicate expert techniques. This review systematically analyzes the integration of EI into endovascular robotics, identifying challenges such as the heterogeneity in validation standards and the gap between human mimicry and machine-native capabilities. Based on this analysis, a conceptual roadmap is proposed that reframes the ultimate objective away from systems that supplant clinical decision-making. This vision of augmented intelligence, where the clinician's role evolves into that of a high-level supervisor, provides a principled foundation for the future of the field.

articles.title: PKR drives neuropathology in a mouse model of Leigh syndrome
articles.content: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a trigger of innate immune responses, yet whether these responses contribute to neurodegeneration remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a cell-type-specific antiviral program in vulnerable GABAergic neurons of Ndufs4-deficient mice and human brain organoids modeling Leigh syndrome. Despite robust type I interferon responses, genetic ablation of innate immune mediators Ifnar1 or Sting1 fails to ameliorate disease progression. Instead, we identify the double-stranded RNA sensor protein kinase R (PKR) as a critical mediator of mitochondrial neuropathology. PKR associates with mitochondrial RNA, while its genetic deletion or silencing delays neurological decline, attenuates neuroinflammation, and extends survival without restoring mitochondrial respiration. PKR deletion also normalizes JNK signaling without detectable global translational repression, suggesting a noncanonical contribution to disease. Together, our findings reveal PKR-mediated antiviral RNA sensing as a pathogenic mechanism in mitochondrial complex I deficiency and highlight PKR as a candidate target for mitochondrial encephalopathies.

articles.title: Systematic and dynamic task coding in the frontal cortex
articles.content: Behavioral flexibility depends on the capacity to form and utilize task representations. Prior work has shown that baseline activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) can differ between two tasks. Comparing more than two tasks makes it possible to ask whether different neuronal populations share a common form of task encoding, that is, a conserved representational geometry across tasks. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform 6 cognitive tasks and recorded spiking activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons in the frontal eye field (FEF) or the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), one area per session. During the fixation period, before any task-specific stimulus appeared, the population activity state already reflected the upcoming task, and task identity could be decoded on single trials. Strikingly, the geometry of the 6 task states was conserved across populations recorded in different sessions, across the two areas, and across the two monkeys. Global signals that differ between tasks, such as expected reward, task difficulty, and attention, measured by reward amount, hit rate, and reaction time, did not fully account for this shared geometry. These findings suggest that the frontal cortex systematically adjusts its population state to encode and prepare for the upcoming task.
articles.author: Park, J., Park, H.-B., Holmes, C. D., Snyder, L. H.

articles.title: The thalamic reticular nucleus provides spatially and temporally tuned inhibition to the lateral geniculate nucleus across species
articles.content: By proposing a role in spatial attention, Francis Crick piqued interest in the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a GABAergic structure that receives input from relay cells projecting to cortex and feeds back inhibition in return. Importantly, predictions of Crick's hypothesis extend beyond attention to suggest that TRN provides selective, localized inhibition to relay cells and, thus, influences sensory processing per se. To ask if this latter role for TRN holds across species, we compared previous recordings from cat with a novel dataset from mouse, focusing on vision. We estimated receptive field size and structure of reticular cells in the visual sector of TRN and of relay cells in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN). Cells in both nuclei encoded specific visual features and had receptive fields of comparable size within binocular visual space. Moreover, paired recordings from both structures suggested that TRN is able to promote burst firing in dLGN in addition to modulating spike rate. Thus, TRN is not only important for attentional regulation, but is also able to make fine-tuned contributions to early sensory processing.

articles.title: Natural language processing for suicidal behavior detection in short Spanish clinical notes from first-contact interviews
articles.content: IntroductionSuicide is a multifactorial phenomenon influenced by social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors, whose early detection remains challenging. According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 years, representing a major public health concern for young populations worldwide. In first-contact clinical settings, screening opportunities are often constrained by limited time, sparse patient information, and operational workflows. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting suicidal behavior from short Spanish-language texts collected during initial screening interviews.MethodsThe dataset comprises 374 anonymized records labeled as “no suicidal behavior,” “ideation,” “planning,” or “attempt,” with a strong imbalance toward “attempt,” reflecting operational clinical usage rather than population-representative sampling. To address data scarcity, we applied data augmentation methods (Easy Data Augmentation for Spanish, backtranslation, and large language model-based synthesis), validated through statistical analysis and clinician-based plausibility assessments.ResultsExploratory analyses revealed highly constrained and overlapping lexical patterns across classes, indicating the challenging nature of the task. A Support Vector Machine achieved 0.53 macro F1 in binary classification (“suicidal behavior” vs. “no behavior”), while BETO, a Spanish BERT model, reached 0.36 macro F1 in multiclass classification. Under the same text-only conditions, human specialists achieved macro F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.15 respectively; however, these results were based on only 20 real texts evaluated with double annotation across five specialists and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.DiscussionAlthough performance is modest compared to studies using full clinical records, these findings suggest that short-text machine learning could support nonspecialists in first-contact settings. Future work should expand datasets and explore multimodal approaches, including voice and text, to improve clinical applicability and early detection.
articles.author: Ansel Y. Rodríguez-González

articles.title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction
articles.content: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures—cells, neurons and vasculature—and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains—from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification—into a single, accessible software environment.
articles.author: Tingwei Quan

articles.title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models
articles.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.

articles.title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action
articles.content: Linking molecular mechanisms with large-scale brain dynamics remains a fundamental challenge in computational psychiatry. Receptor-informed whole-brain models have provided mechanistic insights into pharmacological interventions, yet they have largely relied on single-receptor topographies that cannot explain the collective response of multiple receptor systems. Here, we combined pharmacological resting-state fMRI with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical expression of adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors to investigate the effects of atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that globally elevates catecholaminergic signaling. Using receptor similarity, we first identified a catecholaminergic chemoarchitecture comprising frontal, posterior and temporal networks, providing the neurochemical scaffold for interpreting atomoxetine-induced brain dynamics. Empirically, atomoxetine selectively stabilized functional connectivity dynamics within the posterior catecholaminergic network. Whole-brain modeling revealed that although individual receptor parameters did not differ between conditions, their collective organization converged toward empirical receptor binding affinities. Remarkably, the simulated atomoxetine state was reconstructed from the placebo configuration through a negative reweighting along this receptor-affinity axis. In silico forward modeling showed that this affinity-driven redistribution gave rise to a cortical modulation pattern aligned with a frontal chemoarchitectural gradient, which was sufficient to simulate the observed dynamical and connectivity changes. Together, these findings suggest receptor binding affinity as a key organizing principle linking molecular receptor organization to brain dynamics, providing a model-based, biologically interpretable computational mechanism through which global catecholaminergic perturbations reshape whole-brain function.
articles.author: Gustavo Deco

articles.title: MS-3D-CNN with quantum-inspired chaotic hybrid adaptive wolf-particle swarm optimization for tactical pattern classification in basketball from player tracking data
articles.content: IntroductionAI sport analysis methods have been considerably improved by developments in knowledge of tactically information and its codification. Nevertheless, methods for capturing multi-levels spatio-temporal information for complex team-sport behaviors are still limited. In opposed to motion recognition, which concentrates on movements of individual athlete, tactically pattern classification refers to the recognition of coordinated group actions based mostly on the athlete space-time trajectories.MethodsAn efficient Q16 framework based on MS-3D-CNN and Chaotic Opposition-based Adaptive Wolf-Particle Swarm Optimization (QIC-HAWPSO) for action recognition is proposed in this paper. Parallel multi-scale 3D kernels (three different scales of 3, 5, and 7 frames which correspond to 0.12, 0.20, and 0.28 seconds) are used to learn quick individual actions, complex actions, as well as slow formations. QIC-HAWPSO has chaos opposition-based learning, quantum tunneling adaptive mechanism, and population diversity awareness.ResultsThe framework demonstrated an accuracy of 94.3% on the Basketball-51 dataset (10,311 clips for 8 types of tactical action), leading the current 7 state-of-the-art approaches, such as Game Sense (92.8%), ACA-Net (89.3%), and HAWPSO-3D-CNN (90.1%). Moreover, the inference latency can be evaluated at 34.2 ms clip-1 based on precomputed tracking-grid input and a memory size of 2.4 GB.DiscussionThe classifier will be useful in online coaching, broadcasting, and player analysis, depending on upstream tracking data. It consists of a multi-scale MS-3D-CNN framework, a superior QIC-HAWPSO optimizer, and experimental results that demonstrate the importance of the approach over baseline strategies.
articles.author: Haoyan Liu

articles.title: MA-Pose and DMMS-GCN: skeleton-based martial-arts category recognition with edge-device deployment
articles.content: With the development of visual sensor technology and human pose estimation algorithms, skeleton-based action recognition has received extensive attention in sports analysis and training systems. The recognition of martial-arts actions is difficult because different styles can share similar poses while differing in rhythm and coordination. To support this task, we constructed the Martial Arts Pose (MA-Pose) dataset, which contains 433 source videos across 13 martial arts categories. The 33-landmark sequences include normalized image coordinates and monocular relative depth rather than metric 3D ground truth. We further propose a Dynamic Multi-Stream Multi-Scale Graph Convolutional Network (DMMS-GCN), which integrates joint, bone, and motion features. The model combines physical, learnable, and input-adaptive graph topology with parallel temporal convolutions. With a fixed seed of 42, 346 videos are used for training and 87 for validation, with one center crop and one prediction per validation video. DMMS-GCN correctly classifies 73/87 videos (83.91% Top-1; 83.51% Macro-F1; 95% Wilson confidence interval, 74.78%–90.17%) and retrieves the correct class among the top five for 84/87 videos (96.55%). These values describe development-set performance because model selection and evaluation use the same validation subset. On a Raspberry Pi 4B, pose extraction runs at approximately 10 frames/s and classification of a prepared 150-frame tensor takes approximately 120 ms. Collecting the first 150 processed pose frames takes about 15 s, so the deployment demonstrates edge-device feasibility rather than instantaneous recognition. The source code, model checkpoint, and MA-Pose dataset are publicly available.
articles.author: Shilin Guo

articles.title: Deep reinforcement learning–driven model-based adaptive PID strategy for six-wheeled rocker–bogie mobile platform
articles.content: IntroductionSix-wheel rocker–bogie rovers encounter nonlinear dynamics, variable traction, and wheel slip that can degrade the performance of fixed-gain proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controllers. This study develops a hybrid deep reinforcement learning–PID framework to improve steering and drive control under these conditions.MethodsTwo Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) actor–critic agents adapt the steering and drive PID gains online using low-level dynamic feedback. The reward functions penalise tracking errors, wheel slip, inter-joint mismatch, and abrupt control variations. The framework was evaluated in a three-dimensional MATLAB Simscape Multibody environment incorporating suspension articulation, wheel–terrain contact, and load redistribution. Comparisons with conventional PID and standard DDPG-PID controllers examined tracking accuracy, learning convergence, actuator responses, and disturbance rejection.ResultsThe proposed framework demonstrated more consistent learning convergence, reduced tracking deviations, and smoother actuator torque responses than the baseline controllers. Online gain adaptation improved the steering and drive responses under simulated variations in traction, slip, and payload distribution. The shaped rewards reduced fluctuations in gain updates and critic estimates.DiscussionThese simulation findings support the potential of reinforcement learning–based PID gain adaptation for low-level control of rocker–bogie rovers under uncertain operating conditions. The framework retains the conventional PID structure while introducing data-driven adaptation. Hardware-in-the-loop testing and physical rover experiments remain necessary to establish performance beyond simulation.
articles.author: Hongxue Feng

articles.title: Reliability-aware multimodal sensor fusion for human motion monitoring with safety-constrained neurorobotic feedback in sports training
articles.content: IntroductionEmbodied intelligent systems require reliable perception and safety-constrained feedback mechanisms for human motion understanding under heterogeneous sensing conditions. In this study, volleyball training is considered as a representative dynamic human-motion scenario rather than the sole application objective. The proposed system aims to provide a general neurorobotic perception and feedback framework for complex embodied environments. The framework must infer rapid technical actions while simultaneously tracking fatigue, jump loading, context information, and sensor reliability.MethodsThis study presents an embodied neurorobotic framework that combines a reliability-aware sensor-fusion transformer with a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) estimator. Inertial, pose, plantar-pressure, ultra-wideband, and physiological measurements are synchronized, quality-gated, and exchanged through cross-modal attention before bidirectional temporal reasoning produces action, fatigue, and load estimates. The framework further couples these estimates to a barrier-based safety projection for haptic or robotic feedback. Theoretical analysis establishes a cross-modal perturbation bound and a conditional one-step barrier-satisfaction result under bounded estimation error, bounded disturbance, and maintained projection feasibility. Experiments use an athlete-disjoint, fully reproducible synthetic benchmark with controlled sensor noise and missing-modality conditions.ResultsThe complete model achieves 87.0% accuracy and 0.872 macro-F1, exceeding transformer-only, BiLSTM-only, and no-quality-gate variants. Across the 10 held-out virtual-athlete profiles, accuracy is 0.870 ± 0.086 with a cluster-bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 0.820–0.920. Robustness tests show graceful degradation under moderate corruption, while the illustrative safety-filter simulation prevents all boundary violations observed under the unconstrained policy.DiscussionBecause no human-subject volleyball data are used, these findings establish reproducible computational behavior rather than field safety, injury-prevention efficacy, or clinical validity.
